claims.text: Reported HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
Full ab initio calculations have computational demands that impede rapid alloy discovery.
CALPHAD can be inaccurate when extrapolated to high-entropy alloys and does not directly calculate mechanical properties.
Machine-learning approaches are less reliable for predicting fracture toughness.
The absence of reliable interatomic potentials limits molecular-dynamics prediction of mechanical properties in high-entropy alloys.
A refined interatomic potential can be calibrated specifically to represent the multilevel chemical fluctuations of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The calibrated interatomic potential will accurately capture local elastic moduli and chemical-misfit effects in HfNbTiVAl10.
Atomistic predictions of local elastic and chemical-misfit effects can be passed into continuum stress-field descriptions.
Coupling atomistic distortions to continuum-scale stress distributions bridges ab initio fidelity and continuum efficiency.
The coupled multi-fidelity framework will reduce overall computational demand.
The coupled framework will preserve predictive capability for elastic behavior and fracture behavior.
Predicted Young's modulus will be within 5–10% of full ab initio predictions.
Predicted yield strength will be within 5–10% of full ab initio predictions.
Predicted fracture toughness will be within 5–10% of full ab initio predictions.
The multi-fidelity framework will be at least ten times as computationally efficient as conventional methods.
Reliability will diminish when phase transitions or extreme chemical segregation move the microstructure outside the potential's and continuum model's calibration regime.
Accuracy and efficiency gains will vary with calibration quality and with microstructural variation within HfNbTiVAl10.
The framework's scalability to other alloy systems has not been validated.
A blinded prospective benchmark will compare preregistered predictions of Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness against measurements from independently synthesized samples.
The hypothesis is falsified if errors exceed 15% across multiple samples or if the efficiency gain is below fivefold relative to full ab initio methods.
